read: A fraction tells you how many equal parts to split something into, and how many of those parts you want.
In 3/5, the denominator (5) tells you to split the amount into 5 equal parts. The numerator (3) tells you to take 3 of them.
A bar model shows it clearly: draw a bar for 40, split it into 5 boxes of 8, then shade 3 boxes. The shaded part is 24.
steps: Divide by the denominator: 40 ÷ 5 = 8. So one fifth is 8.
Multiply by the numerator: 8 × 3 = 24. So three fifths is 24.
lesson.check: For a fraction less than 1, your answer must be smaller than the whole.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain to a friend how to find 2/5 of 30, and how you would check your answer.
reflect_ideas: say that you divide by the bottom number first.
say that you then multiply by the top number.
add a check, such as making sure 12 is smaller than 30.

quiz.prompt: What is 1/4 of 36?

options.misconception: You took 4 away. A fraction means splitting into equal parts.
You multiplied by 4. Divide by the denominator instead.
That is the denominator, not the answer.

hints: What does the 4 tell you to do with 36?
Split 36 into 4 equal groups.

quiz.prompt: What is 3/5 of 40?

options.misconception: You found one fifth. Now multiply by 3 to get three fifths.

hints: What does the 5 in 3/5 tell you to do with 40?
Each fifth is 8. You want 3 of them.

quiz.prompt: What is 2/3 of 45?

options.misconception: You found one third. Multiply by 2 for two thirds.

hints: Find one third of 45 first.
One third is 15. How many thirds do you need?

quiz.prompt: Which is larger: 3/4 of 20 or 2/3 of 24?

options.label: 3/4 of 20
options.misconception: 3/4 is a bigger fraction, but 24 is a bigger whole. Work out both: 15 and 16.

quiz.explanation: 3/4 of 20 = 15 and 2/3 of 24 = 16, so 2/3 of 24 is larger.
hints: Work out each one separately.

quiz.prompt: A bag has 60 sweets. Sam eats 5/12 of them. How many are left?

options.misconception: That is how many Sam ate. The question asks how many are left.

hints: What does the 12 in 5/12 tell you to do with the 60 sweets?
Each twelfth is 5 sweets. Sam eats 5 groups.
Sam ate 25. The question asks how many are left.

quiz.prompt: 3/8 of a number is 27. What is the number?

options.misconception: You multiplied 27 by 3. First find one eighth: 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
Nearly there: 9 is one eighth. The whole is 8 eighths.

quiz.explanation: One eighth is 27 ÷ 3 = 9, so the whole is 9 × 8 = 72.
hints: Is 27 the whole amount, or a part of it?
27 is 3 of the 8 parts. How big is one part?

review.prompt: What is 2/5 of 35?
What is 7/10 of 90?
A class has 32 pupils. 3/8 walk to school. How many do not walk?

flashcards.front: What does the denominator tell you?
flashcards.back: How many equal parts the whole is split into

flashcards.front: What does the numerator tell you?
flashcards.back: How many of those parts you take

help.title: Fractions while cooking
help.body: Ask: “The recipe needs 3/4 of 200 g. How much is that?” (Answer: 150 g.) Let your child explain each step out loud.

concepts.title: Finding the whole from a fraction

read: Sometimes you know a part and need the whole. If 2/7 of a number is 18, the 18 is 2 of the 7 equal parts.
Work backwards: find one part, then multiply up to all the parts.
steps: Divide the part by the numerator: 18 ÷ 2 = 9. That is one seventh.
Multiply by the denominator: 9 × 7 = 63. That is the whole.
lesson.check: Your whole must be bigger than the part you started with.
worked_example: 3/4 of a class is 21 pupils. How many in the class?
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain how you would find a number when you know 3/5 of it is 30.
reflect_ideas: say that you divide 30 by 3 first.
say that you then multiply by 5.

quiz.prompt: 1/5 of a number is 7. What is the number?

options.misconception: You found 1/5 of 7. Here 7 is the part, not the whole.

quiz.explanation: One fifth is 7, so the whole is 7 × 5 = 35.
hints: 7 is one of how many equal parts?

quiz.prompt: 2/3 of a number is 20. What is the number?
hints: How much is one third?

quiz.prompt: 3/4 of a class is 21 pupils. How many pupils are in the class?
hints: 21 is 3 quarters. How many is one quarter?

quiz.prompt: 5/6 of a number is 45. What is the number?

options.misconception: That is 5/6 of 45. Here 45 is the part, so work backwards.
9 is one sixth. Multiply by 6 for the whole.

hints: Is 45 the part or the whole?

review.prompt: 1/4 of a number is 12. What is the number?
3/5 of a number is 30. What is the number?
2/9 of a number is 8. What is the number?

flashcards.front: If 1/3 of a number is 5, the number is?
First step to find the whole from 3/4

help.title: Pocket money puzzle
help.body: Say: “I spent 1/4 of my money and it was £5. How much did I have?” (Answer: £20.) Ask how they worked it out.

read: You can only add fractions when the parts are the same size, so the denominators must match.
Change one or both fractions into equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then add the numerators.
steps: Find a common denominator: for 2/3 + 1/6, use sixths.
Convert: 2/3 = 4/6.
Add the numerators: 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
lesson.check: Never add the denominators: the size of the parts does not change.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why 1/2 + 1/4 is not 2/6.
reflect_ideas: explain that the parts must be the same size first.

options.misconception: You added the tops and the bottoms. Make the denominators match first.

hints: Can you write 1/2 in quarters?

quiz.prompt: 2/3 + 1/6 = ? (write it as a fraction, like 1/2)
hints: Write 2/3 in sixths.

quiz.prompt: 3/5 + 1/10 = ? (write it as a fraction)
hints: Write 3/5 in tenths.

quiz.prompt: 1/3 + 1/4 = ? (write it as a fraction)
hints: Both 3 and 4 go into 12.

review.prompt: Which is the first step for 1/5 + 3/10?

options.label: Add 5 and 10
options.misconception: Denominators are never added.

flashcards.back: No: make them the same first

help.title: Pizza fractions
help.body: Cut a pizza or a sheet of paper into 8. Ask: “If I eat 1/4 and you eat 1/8, how much is gone?” (Answer: 3/8.)

read: Per cent means out of 100. 10% is one tenth, 25% is one quarter and 50% is one half.
To find other percentages, build them from 10% and 1%.
steps: Find 10% by dividing by 10.
Build up: 15% = 10% + 5% (half of 10%).
lesson.check: 50% must be half; 100% is the whole amount.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain two ways to find 25% of 360.

quiz.prompt: What is 25% of 360?

options.misconception: That is 10%. 25% is one quarter.
You subtracted 25.

hints: What fraction is 25%?

quiz.prompt: What is 10% of 70?
hints: 10% is one tenth.

quiz.prompt: What is 15% of 80?
hints: Find 10% first, then half of it.

quiz.prompt: What is 60% of 45?
hints: Find 10% of 45 first.

review.prompt: What is 50% of 64?
What is 20% of 150?
What is 75% of 120?

help.title: Shopping sale
help.body: In a shop or online, ask: “This £40 coat has 25% off. How much do we save?” (Answer: £10.)

read: The arithmetic paper tests fast, accurate written methods: column addition and subtraction, short and long multiplication, and division.
Line digits up by place value, and estimate first so you can spot a wrong answer.
steps: Calculate carefully, then compare with your estimate.
lesson.check: If your answer is far from your estimate, check each column.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain how estimating helps you check a long multiplication.
reflect_ideas: say that you round the numbers first.

help.title: Number talk at dinner
help.body: Ask your child to estimate the total of a shopping receipt before you add it up exactly.

courses.title: English
courses.subject: English
courses.exam: KS2 grammar, punctuation and spelling test

read: In an active sentence, the subject does the action: “The dog chased the cat.”
In a passive sentence, the subject has the action done to it: “The cat was chased by the dog.”
Writers choose the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant or something they want to hide. News reports often say “Three shops were damaged” because the damage matters most.
steps: Find the object (the thing the action is done to).
Move it to the front as the new subject.
Add a form of be plus the past participle: was cooked, were taken, has been repaired.
lesson.check: “Tom was running” is not passive: Tom is still doing the action.
worked_example: The meal was cooked by the chef.
The library was closed by the council.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Write one active sentence about your school and turn it into the passive. Which would a head teacher use in a letter about a broken window, and why?
reflect_ideas: use a form of be, such as was, in your passive sentence.
say why the doer might be left out.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

options.label: Tom broke the window.
options.misconception: Here Tom does the action, so it is active.

options.label: The window broke.
options.misconception: No one does anything to the window here; it is active, even without a doer.

options.label: Tom was breaking the window.
options.misconception: “Was” does not make a sentence passive: Tom is still the doer.

quiz.explanation: In “The window was broken” the action is done to the window.
hints: Who or what is the action done to?

quiz.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: “The chef cooked the meal.”
quiz.answer: The meal was cooked by the chef.|The meal was cooked.
quiz.explanation: The object moves to the front and the verb becomes was cooked.
hints: What is the thing being cooked?
Start with “The meal”.
Add was plus the past participle of cook.

quiz.prompt: Complete with the passive form of deliver: “The parcels ___ every morning.”
hints: Parcels is plural and it happens every morning.

quiz.prompt: In “The cake was eaten by the children”, who did the eating?

options.label: the cake
options.misconception: The cake is the subject, but the children did the action.

review.prompt: Active or passive: “The song was written in 1990.”

options.label: Active
options.misconception: The song had the action done to it.

review.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: “Wasps stung the gardener.”
review.answer: The gardener was stung by wasps.|The gardener was stung.

review.prompt: Active or passive: “The children were laughing.”

options.label: Passive
options.misconception: “Were” does not make it passive: the children are doing the laughing.

flashcards.back: a form of be + past participle

help.title: Headline hunt
help.body: Find a news headline together and ask: “Do we know who did it?” “Window smashed at school” hides the doer. That is the passive voice.

read: A relative clause adds information about a noun. It usually starts with a relative pronoun: who, which, that, whose, where or when.
“The boy who won the race smiled.” The clause “who won the race” tells us which boy.
steps: Use who for people, which for things, whose for belonging.
Use where for places and when for times.
lesson.check: Take the clause out: the main sentence should still make sense.
worked_example: The book ___ I borrowed was great.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Write a sentence about your town with a relative clause starting with where.

quiz.prompt: Which word is the relative pronoun? “The boy who won the race smiled.”
Choose the word: “The dog ___ bone was buried barked.”

options.label: who's
options.misconception: Who's means who is.

options.label: which
options.misconception: Use whose to show belonging.

quiz.prompt: Fill the gap: “The house ___ I grew up is now a shop.”
Which sentence contains a relative clause?

options.label: My aunt lives in Leeds.
options.misconception: There is no clause adding information about a noun.

options.label: My aunt, who lives in Leeds, is visiting.
My aunt is visiting on Friday.
options.misconception: On Friday is a phrase about time, not a relative clause.

quiz.answer: My aunt, who lives in Leeds, is visiting.
quiz.explanation: “who lives in Leeds” adds information about my aunt.

review.prompt: Relative pronoun for a place?
Relative pronoun for belonging?
Find the relative pronoun: “The cake that Mum made was delicious.”

flashcards.back: who, which, that, whose, where, when

help.title: Who, which, where game
help.body: On a walk, take turns describing things with who, which or where: “That is the shop where we buy bread.”

read: An apostrophe can show that something belongs to someone.
One owner: add ’s (the dog’s bowl). Plural owner ending in s: add ’ after the s (the dogs’ bowls). Plural not ending in s: add ’s (the children’s toys).
steps: Decide who the owner is and whether there is one or more.
Write the owner word, then add the apostrophe in the right place.
lesson.check: Its (belonging) has no apostrophe; it’s means it is.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain the difference between its and it’s.
reflect_ideas: say that it's means it is.

quiz.prompt: Write with an apostrophe: the bowl belonging to one dog
Write with an apostrophe: the coats of the girls
Write with an apostrophe: the toys of the children
quiz.explanation: Children does not end in s: children’s.

quiz.prompt: Choose: “The cat licked ___ paw.”

options.label: it's
options.misconception: It's means it is. Belonging uses its.

review.prompt: the hat of the man
the bags of the teachers
“___ raining.”

options.label: Its
options.misconception: It is raining needs it's.

help.title: Label spotting
help.body: Look at shop signs together and spot apostrophes. Are they right? (“Carrot’s £1” is a common mistake.)

read: Modal verbs show how likely something is or whether it must happen: can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must.
“It might rain” is less certain than “It will rain”.
steps: Decide how certain or necessary the action is.
Choose the modal verb that matches.
lesson.check: Must and will show the most certainty or need; might and may show possibility.
worked_example: You ___ wear a helmet. It’s the law.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Write two sentences about tomorrow’s weather, one certain and one uncertain.
reflect_ideas: use will for the certain one.
use might for the uncertain one.

quiz.prompt: Which modal verb shows the most certainty?

options.label: might
options.misconception: Might shows possibility, not certainty.

options.label: could
options.misconception: Could shows possibility.

quiz.prompt: Fill the gap: “You ___ wear a helmet; it’s the law.”
quiz.explanation: It is a rule, so must.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence shows possibility?

options.label: We will go to the park.
options.misconception: Will is certain.

options.label: We might go to the park.
We must go to the park.
options.misconception: Must shows need.

quiz.answer: We might go to the park.

review.prompt: Modal verb for possibility, starting with m
Most certain:

options.label: may
options.misconception: May is possible, not certain.

review.prompt: Fill: “You ___ finish your homework before you play.” (it is required)

help.title: Weather forecast
help.body: Ask your child to read tomorrow’s forecast and say it with modal verbs: “It might rain, but it will be windy.”

read: Words like all, some and no change what we can be sure of.
“All dogs are animals. Rex is a dog.” So Rex must be an animal.
“All cats have tails. Bella has a tail.” Is Bella a cat? Not necessarily: dogs and mice have tails too.
steps: Draw a Venn diagram: put the smaller group inside the bigger one.
Ask: must it be true, or only might it be true?
lesson.check: “All A are B” does not mean “all B are A”.
worked_example: No fish can fly. Some pets are fish.
So some pets cannot fly: must be true.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Write your own “All… This is… So…” argument that is correct, and one that is a trap.
reflect_ideas: use the word all in your argument.
explain why the trap does not have to be true.

quiz.prompt: All roses are flowers. This is a rose. Must it be a flower?

options.label: No
options.misconception: If all roses are flowers, any rose is a flower.

quiz.prompt: All squares have four sides. This shape has four sides. Must it be a square?

options.label: Yes
options.misconception: All squares have four sides, but other shapes do too, like rectangles.

quiz.explanation: No: it could be a rectangle or a rhombus.

quiz.prompt: No fish can fly. Some pets are fish. Must some pets be unable to fly?

options.label: No
options.misconception: The pets that are fish cannot fly, so some pets cannot fly.

quiz.prompt: Some children in the class like football. Does that mean some do not?

options.label: Yes
options.misconception: Some can still mean all of them. We cannot be sure.

review.prompt: All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. Must it have feathers?

options.label: No
options.misconception: All birds have feathers.

review.prompt: All triangles have three sides. This shape has three sides. Must it be a triangle?

options.label: No
options.misconception: A shape with three straight sides is a triangle.

review.prompt: All cats have whiskers. Max has whiskers. Must Max be a cat?

options.label: Yes
options.misconception: Dogs and rabbits have whiskers too.

flashcards.front: All A are B. Does it mean all B are A?

help.title: Must or might?
help.body: At dinner, say a rule like “All our plates are white” and test it: “This is white. Must it be our plate?”

read: A logic grid puzzle gives clues; each clue rules out possibilities.
Draw a grid with people down the side and options along the top. Put a cross for impossible, a tick for certain.
steps: Use the definite clues first.
When a row has one gap left, it must be the answer.
lesson.check: Every row and column has exactly one tick.
worked_example: Ava, Ben and Cal have a cat, dog and fish. Ava does not have the dog. Ben has the fish.
Ben: fish. Ava: cat. Cal: dog.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain the first clue you used in a logic grid and why.
reflect_ideas: say why you start with the definite clue.

quiz.prompt: Ava, Ben and Cal have a cat, a dog and a fish. Ava does not have the dog. Ben has the fish. Who has the dog?

options.label: Ava
options.misconception: The clue says Ava does not have the dog.

options.label: Ben
options.misconception: Ben has the fish.

quiz.explanation: Ben has the fish, Ava is not the dog, so Cal.

quiz.prompt: Three friends sit in a row. Jo is in the middle. Kim is not on the left. Where is Kim?

options.label: In the middle
options.misconception: Jo is in the middle.

options.label: On the left
options.misconception: The clue says Kim is not on the left.

quiz.explanation: Only the right is left for Kim.

quiz.prompt: In a grid, a row has crosses in all boxes but one. What goes in the last box?

options.label: A cross
options.misconception: Each row needs exactly one tick.

quiz.explanation: The last box must be a tick.

review.prompt: Mia likes red or blue. She does not like red. Which does she like?

options.label: Red
options.misconception: The clue rules out red.

review.prompt: Two clues say Sam is not first and not third of three. Where is Sam?

options.label: First
options.misconception: Ruled out.

review.prompt: How many ticks in each row of a logic grid?

options.label: Two
options.misconception: Each person has exactly one option.

help.title: Who has what?
help.body: Make a quick puzzle with family members and their favourite drinks, and let your child solve it with a grid.

read: A fact can be checked and shown to be true or false. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
Words like best, worst, should and I think often signal opinions.
steps: Ask: could I check this?
Look for feeling words.
lesson.check: A fact can be wrong and still be a statement of fact.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Find one fact and one opinion in an advert and explain which is which.
reflect_ideas: say how you could check the fact.

quiz.prompt: Fact or opinion: “The Thames flows through London.”

options.label: Opinion
options.misconception: You can check this on a map.

quiz.prompt: Fact or opinion: “Maths is the most fun subject.”

options.label: Fact
options.misconception: People disagree; it cannot be proved.

quiz.prompt: Which word often signals an opinion?

options.label: measured
options.misconception: Measured suggests something checked.

review.prompt: Fact or opinion: “There are 7 days in a week.”

options.label: Opinion
options.misconception: It can be checked.

review.prompt: Fact or opinion: “Summer is better than winter.”

options.label: Fact
options.misconception: This is what someone thinks.

review.prompt: “This shop has the friendliest staff.” is...

options.label: Fact
options.misconception: Friendliest is a judgement.

help.title: Advert detective
help.body: Watch an advert together and sort its claims into facts and opinions.

read: Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
In pure water, water moves into cells. Animal cells swell and may burst; plant cells become turgid because the cell wall stops them bursting.
In a concentrated solution, water moves out. Animal cells shrink; plant cells become flaccid and can plasmolyse.
steps: Required practical: weigh potato cylinders, leave them in sugar solutions, blot dry, reweigh.
Calculate % change in mass = change ÷ start mass × 100.
Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses zero matches the cell concentration.
lesson.check: Only water moves in osmosis, not the solute.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why salting a slug harms it, using the word osmosis.

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct definition of osmosis?

options.label: Movement of sugar from a concentrated to a dilute solution
options.misconception: Osmosis is about water, not the solute.

options.label: Diffusion of water from a dilute to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
Diffusion of water from a concentrated to a dilute solution
options.misconception: The direction is reversed: water moves to the more concentrated side.

quiz.answer: Diffusion of water from a dilute to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane

quiz.prompt: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens?

options.label: It shrinks
options.misconception: Water moves in, not out, in pure water.

options.label: It becomes turgid
options.misconception: Turgid describes plant cells with a cell wall.

quiz.explanation: Water enters; no cell wall to stop it.

quiz.prompt: A potato cylinder is left in 1.0 mol/dm³ sugar solution. Its mass will...

options.label: Increase
options.misconception: The solution is more concentrated, so water leaves the potato.

quiz.prompt: A cylinder goes from 2.50 g to 2.20 g. Calculate the % change in mass.

options.misconception: The mass went down, so the change is negative.
Divide by the starting mass, 2.50.

hints: Change = end minus start.
Divide the change by the starting mass, not the end mass.

review.prompt: In osmosis, water moves to the more...

options.label: dilute solution
options.misconception: Water moves from dilute to concentrated.

review.prompt: Name the state of a plant cell full of water.
A cylinder goes from 3.20 g to 3.60 g. % change?

flashcards.back: Diffusion of water from dilute to concentrated across a partially permeable membrane

help.title: Kitchen osmosis
help.body: Put a carrot stick in salty water and one in plain water overnight. Ask your child to explain the difference using osmosis.

read: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
It is passive: it needs no energy from the cell. Oxygen and carbon dioxide move into and out of cells by diffusion.
steps: Rate increases with a bigger concentration gradient.
Rate increases with higher temperature and a larger surface area.
lesson.check: Diffusion continues until concentrations are equal.
worked_example: Moves from air sacs (high) into the blood (low).
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why the lungs have many small air sacs.

quiz.prompt: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from...

options.label: low to high concentration
options.misconception: That would need energy: it is active transport.

quiz.prompt: Which increases the rate of diffusion?

options.label: A smaller surface area
options.misconception: Smaller area slows diffusion.

quiz.prompt: Does diffusion need energy from respiration?

options.label: Yes
options.misconception: Diffusion is passive.

review.prompt: Is diffusion active or passive?
Oxygen moves into the blood in the lungs because...

options.label: the blood pulls it in
options.misconception: There is no pulling: it is a concentration gradient.

options.label: its concentration is lower in the blood

review.answer: its concentration is lower in the blood

review.prompt: A steeper concentration gradient makes diffusion...

options.label: slower
options.misconception: Bigger difference, faster diffusion.

help.title: Perfume test
help.body: Spray perfume in a corner and time how long until your child smells it across the room. Ask why it spreads.

read: Animal and plant cells both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.
Plant cells also have a cell wall made of cellulose, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.
steps: Learn the parts both cells share.
Learn the three extra plant parts: cell wall, chloroplasts, permanent vacuole.
lesson.check: Not every plant cell has chloroplasts: root cells do not.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why root hair cells do not need chloroplasts.
reflect_ideas: link chloroplasts to light and photosynthesis.

quiz.prompt: Which part is found in plant cells but not animal cells?

options.label: Cell membrane
options.misconception: Both have a cell membrane.

options.label: Mitochondria
options.misconception: Both have mitochondria.

quiz.prompt: Where does photosynthesis happen?

options.label: Mitochondria
options.misconception: Mitochondria are for respiration.

quiz.prompt: What controls the activities of the cell?

review.prompt: Where does aerobic respiration happen?
Cell walls are made of...

options.label: glucose
options.misconception: Glucose is a sugar used in respiration.

review.prompt: Do animal cells have a permanent vacuole?

options.label: Yes
options.misconception: Only plant cells have a permanent vacuole.

help.title: Cell salad
help.body: While cooking, ask your child which parts of a plant cell would be in a lettuce leaf, and which would not be in a potato.

read: Speed tells you how far something travels each second: speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s).
On a distance–time graph, the gradient is the speed. A horizontal line means the object is stationary. A steeper line is faster.
Typical speeds: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s, sound in air about 330 m/s.
steps: Choose the equation and rearrange if needed.
Check the units match: km/h to m/s means × 1000 ÷ 3600.
Substitute and give the unit.
lesson.check: A flat line is stationary, not constant speed.
worked_example: A runner covers 400 m in 80 s
lesson.reflect_prompt: Describe a journey you made today as a distance–time graph.
reflect_ideas: say where the line is flat.

quiz.prompt: A car travels 150 m in 6 s. What is its speed in m/s?

options.misconception: You multiplied. Divide distance by time.

hints: Speed = distance ÷ time.

quiz.prompt: A runner moves at 4 m/s. How long does it take to run 1000 m, in seconds?

options.misconception: You multiplied. Divide distance by speed.

hints: Time = distance ÷ speed.

quiz.prompt: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

options.misconception: You still need to divide by 3600.

hints: How many metres in a kilometre?
How many seconds in an hour?

quiz.prompt: What does a horizontal line on a distance–time graph show?

options.label: Constant speed
options.misconception: That is a horizontal line on a speed–time graph, not distance–time.

review.prompt: What does the gradient of a distance–time graph show?
A bus travels 1200 m in 120 s. Speed in m/s?
Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far does it travel in 3 s, in metres?

help.title: Walking speed check
help.body: Time a family walk between two lamp posts and work out walking speed together in m/s.

read: Kinetic energy is the energy stored in a moving object: E = ½ × m × v², in joules.
Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times bigger, because speed is squared.
steps: Square the speed first.
Multiply by the mass and by ½.
lesson.check: Mass in kg, speed in m/s, energy in J.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why speed matters more than mass for kinetic energy.

quiz.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s, in J.

options.misconception: You forgot to square the speed.

hints: Square the speed first.

quiz.prompt: A 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s. Kinetic energy in J?
If speed doubles, kinetic energy...

options.label: doubles
options.misconception: Speed is squared, so 2² = 4.

review.prompt: A 4 kg object at 2 m/s. KE in J?
Unit of energy?
A 0.5 kg ball at 4 m/s. KE in J?

help.title: Car safety talk
help.body: Ask why speed limits near schools are low. (Doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy to stop.)

read: Potential difference V (volts) = current I (amps) × resistance R (ohms): V = I × R.
For a fixed resistor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to potential difference.
steps: Write the equation and rearrange if needed.
Substitute with units.
lesson.check: Check units: V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain what happens to current if resistance goes up and voltage stays the same.

quiz.prompt: A current of 0.5 A flows through a 12 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference in V?
A 9 V battery drives 3 A through a resistor. Resistance in Ω?
If resistance increases and p.d. stays the same, current...

options.label: increases
options.misconception: I = V ÷ R, so a bigger R gives a smaller I.

review.prompt: I = 2 A, R = 5 Ω. V?
V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω. I in A?
Unit of resistance?

help.title: Plug check
help.body: Look at the label on a phone charger together and find the voltage and current. Ask your child what they mean.

read: A for loop repeats a block of code once for each value in a sequence. The indented lines are the loop body.
range(3) gives 0, 1, 2: it starts at 0 and stops before 3. range(start, stop, step) gives more control: range(2, 10, 3) gives 2, 5, 8.
Loops often build up a result: start a total at 0 before the loop, then add to it inside.
steps: for i in range(1, 11):
total = total + i
print(total)  # 55
lesson.check: The stop value is never included. To count 1 to 5, use range(1, 6).
worked_example: for i in range(1, 4): print("*" * i)
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why range(1, 6) gives five numbers but stops at 5.
reflect_ideas: say that the stop value is not included.
say that the start is included.

quiz.prompt: What does for i in range(3): print(i) output?

options.misconception: range starts at 0 unless you give a start.
The stop value 3 is not included.

quiz.prompt: What values does range(2, 10, 3) produce?

options.misconception: 11 is past the stop value.
It starts at 2, the first argument.

quiz.prompt: Which call gives the numbers 1 to 5?

options.label: range(1, 5)
options.misconception: Stop is not included, so this ends at 4.

options.label: range(5)
options.misconception: This gives 0 to 4.

quiz.prompt: x = 0, then for i in range(4): x += i, then print(x). What is printed?

options.misconception: range(4) is 0, 1, 2, 3, not 1 to 4.

hints: Which values does range(4) give?

review.prompt: What does range(4) produce? (write like 0, 1, 2)
Write the range call for 5, 10, 15, 20.
total = 0, for n in range(1, 101): total += n. What is total?

help.title: Teach-back
help.body: Ask your child to show you a loop they wrote and explain what each line does. You don’t need to know Python to ask good questions.

read: A variable is a named store for a value: score = 10.
Common data types: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text in quotes) and bool (True or False).
steps: Choose a clear name.
Use input() to read text; convert with int() if you need a number.
lesson.check: "5" is text; 5 is a number.
worked_example: Converts the text typed to an int.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain why "3" + "4" gives "34" in Python.

quiz.prompt: What data type is 3.5?

options.label: int
options.misconception: int is for whole numbers.

quiz.prompt: What does print("3" + "4") output?

options.misconception: These are strings, so + joins them.

quiz.prompt: Which converts the text "12" to a number?

options.label: str(12)
options.misconception: str turns a number into text.

review.prompt: Data type of True?
Data type of "hello"?
x = 5, x = x + 2, print(x)

help.title: Type sorting
help.body: Ask your child whether your phone number, age and name would be stored as int or str in a program, and why.

read: An if statement runs code only when a condition is True. elif checks another condition; else runs when none are True.
Comparison operators: == equal, != not equal, <, >, <=, >=.
steps: if score >= 50:
print("Pass")
else:
print("Try again")
lesson.check: Use == to compare; = assigns a value.
worked_example: if mark >= 70: print("A") elif mark >= 50: print("B") else: print("C")
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain the difference between = and == in Python.

quiz.prompt: Which operator checks if two values are equal?

options.misconception: = assigns a value; it does not compare.

quiz.prompt: x = 7. if x > 5: print("big") else: print("small"). Output?

options.label: small
options.misconception: 7 is greater than 5.

quiz.prompt: What runs when no if or elif condition is True?

options.label: elif
options.misconception: elif needs its own condition to be True.

review.prompt: Not equal operator?
x = 3. if x >= 3: output "yes"?

options.label: nothing
options.misconception: 3 >= 3 is True.

review.prompt: Which keyword checks a second condition?

options.label: else
options.misconception: else has no condition.

help.title: If-then rules
help.body: Turn a household rule into an if statement together: “if it is raining: take a coat”.

read: A meander is a large bend in a river, mostly in the middle and lower course.
Water flows fastest on the outside of a bend, eroding the bank by hydraulic action and abrasion to form a river cliff. On the inside, slower water deposits sediment as a slip-off slope.
Over time the neck between two bends narrows. In a flood the river cuts through the neck; deposition seals off the old bend, leaving an ox-bow lake.
steps: Outside bend: fastest flow, erosion, river cliff.
Inside bend: slowest flow, deposition, slip-off slope.
Flood cuts the neck; deposition seals the old meander.
lesson.check: Erosion is on the outside of the bend, not the inside.
worked_example: Erosion on outer bends narrows the neck; a flood cuts through; deposition seals the old channel; the cut-off bend becomes an ox-bow lake.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Mark where you would stand to see erosion and where to see deposition on a meander, and explain why.
reflect_ideas: say erosion is on the outside bend.
say deposition is on the inside bend.
link it to the speed or energy of the water.

quiz.prompt: On which side of a meander is the river cliff?

options.label: The inside bend
options.misconception: The inside bend has slow water and deposition.

quiz.prompt: Why does deposition happen on the inside bend?

options.label: It is sheltered from the wind
options.misconception: Wind is not the reason: it is the water's speed and energy.

options.label: The water is slower and has less energy

quiz.answer: The water is slower and has less energy
quiz.explanation: Less energy, so sediment is dropped.

quiz.prompt: What usually cuts through a meander neck?

options.label: Tidal waves
options.misconception: Rivers in the middle and lower course cut through in floods.

quiz.prompt: Name the erosion process where the force of water pushes air into cracks.

options.label: Attrition
options.misconception: Attrition is rocks hitting each other.

review.prompt: Landform on the outside of a meander bend?
Landform on the inside of a meander bend?
Ox-bow lakes are most common in the...

options.label: upper course
options.misconception: The upper course has V-shaped valleys and waterfalls.

help.title: River walk
help.body: On a walk by a river or stream, ask your child to point out where the water is fastest and where sand or pebbles build up.

read: Rivers erode in four ways: hydraulic action (force of water), abrasion (rocks scraping the bed and banks), attrition (rocks hitting each other and becoming smaller and rounder) and solution (rocks dissolving).
steps: Learn each process with one example.
Abrasion is usually the most effective process.
lesson.check: Attrition wears the load, not the banks.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain the difference between abrasion and attrition.
reflect_ideas: say abrasion wears the bed and banks.
say attrition is rocks hitting each other.

quiz.prompt: Which process makes river stones smaller and rounder?

options.label: Abrasion
options.misconception: Abrasion wears the bed and banks.

quiz.prompt: Which process dissolves limestone?

options.label: Hydraulic action
options.misconception: Hydraulic action is the force of water.

quiz.prompt: Rocks scraping the river bed is...

options.label: Attrition
options.misconception: Attrition is rocks hitting each other.

review.prompt: Erosion by the force of water?
Rocks dissolving?
Rocks knocking into each other?

help.title: Pebble hunt
help.body: Compare pebbles from a beach or river with sharp stones from a path. Ask your child which erosion process made them round.

read: Grid references give a location on a map. Read across first (eastings), then up (northings): “along the corridor and up the stairs”.
A four-figure reference names a square. A six-figure reference adds tenths for a precise point.
steps: Find the bottom-left corner of the square.
Write the easting, then the northing.
For six figures, estimate tenths across and up.
lesson.check: Always go along before up.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Explain how to give a six-figure grid reference.

quiz.prompt: A square's bottom-left corner is at easting 34 and northing 72. Four-figure reference?
Which do you read first?

options.label: Northings (up)
options.misconception: Along the corridor first, then up the stairs.

quiz.prompt: How many figures pinpoint a precise location?

options.label: Four
options.misconception: Four figures give a whole square.

review.prompt: Easting 12, northing 45: four-figure reference?
Grid lines going up the map are...

options.label: northings
options.misconception: Lines running up the map are numbered along the bottom: eastings.

review.prompt: A four-figure reference describes a...

options.label: point
options.misconception: A point needs six figures.

flashcards.back: Along the corridor, up the stairs

help.title: Map treasure hunt
help.body: Use a printed or online OS map of your area and ask your child for the grid reference of your house or school.

read: A conditional says: if P is true, then Q is true (P → Q). It is broken only when P is true and Q is false.
Modus ponens (P, so Q) and modus tollens (not Q, so not P) are valid. Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (not P, so not Q) are invalid.
Valid means the conclusion must follow if the premises are true. Sound means valid and the premises really are true.
steps: Write the rule as P → Q.
Identify which part the evidence is about.
Check it against the four forms.
lesson.check: An if…then is broken only when the if is true and the then is false.
worked_example: Cards E, K, 4, 7. Rule: if vowel, then even on the back.
Turn E (could have odd) and 7 (could have a vowel).
lesson.reflect_prompt: Write a rule from your own life and give one case that breaks it and one that does not.
reflect_ideas: write the rule as an if...then sentence.

quiz.prompt: In the truth table for P → Q, how many rows are false?

options.misconception: That is the AND table. P → Q is false only once.

quiz.explanation: Only P true and Q false.

quiz.prompt: “If you are in Year 11, you sit GCSEs. Kai sits GCSEs. So Kai is in Year 11.”

options.label: Valid
options.misconception: This is affirming the consequent: other people sit GCSEs too.

quiz.prompt: “If you are in Year 11, you sit GCSEs. Jo does not sit GCSEs. So Jo is not in Year 11.”

options.label: Invalid
options.misconception: This is modus tollens, which is valid.

quiz.prompt: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test finds 99% of cases but gives false positives 5% of the time. Roughly what is the chance a positive person has the disease?

options.label: About 99%
options.misconception: This ignores the base rate: most positives come from the many healthy people.

options.label: About 5%
options.misconception: That is the false positive rate, not the answer.

quiz.explanation: In 100 000 people: 99 true positives and about 4995 false positives, so about 1.9%.

review.prompt: When is P → Q false?

options.label: P false and Q true
options.misconception: A false if makes no promise.

review.prompt: “If it snows, school closes. School closed. So it snowed.”

options.label: Valid
options.misconception: Affirming the consequent.

review.prompt: Can a valid argument have a false conclusion?

options.label: No
options.misconception: Validity is about form, not truth.

options.label: Yes, if a premise is false

review.answer: Yes, if a premise is false

flashcards.back: P is true and Q is false
If P then Q; not Q; so not P

help.title: Rule breakers
help.body: Pick a family rule (“If it’s a school night, screens off at 9”) and ask your child which situations would break it.

read: A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument look stronger than it is.

Ad hominem attacks the person. Straw man twists the other view. False dilemma offers only two options. Slippery slope claims an extreme chain without evidence. Bandwagon says many people believe it so it is true. Correlation as causation assumes two things that happen together are cause and effect.
steps: Find the conclusion.
Ask what the reasons really show.
Name the flaw.
lesson.check: Naming the fallacy is not enough: say why the reasoning fails.
worked_example: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise.
Correlation as causation: hot weather drives both.
lesson.reflect_prompt: Find an advert that uses a fallacy and rewrite it as a fair argument.

quiz.prompt: “You can’t trust Sam’s argument for recycling; he once dropped litter.”

options.label: Straw man
options.misconception: Sam's view is not twisted; Sam himself is attacked.

quiz.prompt: “Either we cancel sports day or pupils will get sunburn.”

options.label: Slippery slope
options.misconception: There is no chain of events, just two options.

quiz.prompt: “Pupils who eat breakfast get better grades, so breakfast makes you clever.”

options.label: Bandwagon
options.misconception: No appeal to popularity here.

review.prompt: “Everyone is buying these trainers, so they must be best.”

options.label: Ad hominem
options.misconception: No person is attacked.

review.prompt: “If we allow trainers, soon there will be no uniform at all.”

options.label: False dilemma
options.misconception: It is a chain of consequences.

review.prompt: A: “We need more trees.” B: “So you want no space to play?”

options.label: Ad hominem
options.misconception: B twists A's view rather than attacking A.

flashcards.back: Attacking the person, not the argument

help.title: Debate dinner
help.body: Pick a light topic and take turns making arguments; the others spot any fallacies.
